# Which forecaster should I use?

Answer four questions about your data (three for a category). You get the forecasters to compare first, the baseline to compare them with and a script that runs as it is.

<div class="sk-finder" id="sk-finder" data-src="../javascripts/finder-data.json">
<noscript>The interactive finder needs JavaScript. The rules and an example script are below.</noscript>
</div>

## How we chose these rules

<!-- FORECASTER-FINDER:EVIDENCE:START - generated by tools/docs/forecaster_finder/build.py, do not edit by hand -->
Each model was run with the same backtesting on 26 public datasets, with every model using all the data before each test period. The error is the MASE (the mean absolute error, scaled so that datasets can be compared). Each row counts datasets, not runs. Some datasets are in more than one row, with and without their known variables or with one and several series, so the rows add up to 33 cases.

| Your data | Datasets | Lower error: Chronos-2 | Lower error: LightGBM | LightGBM worse than the baseline |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| One series, nothing known in advance | 16 | 14 of 16 | 2 of 16 | 7 of 16 |
| One series, variables known in advance | 7 | 5 of 7 | 2 of 7 | 1 of 7 |
| Several series | 10 | 8 of 10 | 2 of 10 | 2 of 10 |

- Chronos-2 did not do worse than the baseline in any dataset.
- With an automatic search of 20 trials, LightGBM improved in 18 of the 33 cases and had a lower error than Chronos-2 in 7.
- In the 8 monthly and quarterly datasets with one series, ARIMA had a lower error than LightGBM in 6 and than Chronos-2 in 3.
<!-- FORECASTER-FINDER:EVIDENCE:END -->

Except in that search, each model has one configuration, without tuning: Chronos-2 is its smallest version, and LightGBM uses the settings of the scripts of this page. The datasets are public, so Chronos-2 may have seen some of them during its training, which would make its results optimistic. A model trained with variables that capture what you know about your problem can do better than these figures, which is why LightGBM is always one of the two candidates. The scripts and results of the study are in [benchmarks/forecaster_finder](https://github.com/skforecast/skforecast/tree/main/benchmarks/forecaster_finder).

The guide [Comparing forecasting models](../user_guides/comparing-forecasting-models.ipynb) looks at three datasets in detail. A single dataset can go against these counts: in its monthly example ARIMA is behind LightGBM, and with exogenous variables LightGBM is ahead of Chronos-2.

## The rules at a glance

<!-- FORECASTER-FINDER:RULES:START - generated by tools/docs/forecaster_finder/build.py, do not edit by hand -->
| Your data | Forecasters to compare | Baseline |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A number, one series | [`ForecasterRecursive`](../user_guides/autoregressive-forecaster.ipynb) with LightGBM and [`ForecasterFoundation`](../user_guides/foundation-forecasting-models.ipynb) with Chronos-2 | [`ForecasterEquivalentDate`](../user_guides/forecasting-baseline.ipynb): the value one season before |
| A number, one monthly or quarterly series | The same two, and [`ForecasterStats`](../user_guides/forecasting-sarimax-arima.ipynb) with ARIMA as a reference | [`ForecasterEquivalentDate`](../user_guides/forecasting-baseline.ipynb): the value one season before |
| A number, several series | [`ForecasterRecursiveMultiSeries`](../user_guides/independent-multi-time-series-forecasting.ipynb) with LightGBM and [`ForecasterFoundation`](../user_guides/foundation-forecasting-models.ipynb) with Chronos-2 | [`ForecasterEquivalentDate`](../user_guides/forecasting-baseline.ipynb), one per series |
| A category | [`ForecasterRecursiveClassifier`](../user_guides/autoregressive-classification-forecasting.ipynb) with a LightGBM classifier | The category one season before (`y.shift(season)`) |

If you know variables in advance (holidays, promotions, prices), pass them as `exog` to the forecasters. ARIMA is run without them.

The scripts need at least 2 weeks of hourly data, 3 months of daily data, 2 years of weekly data, 3 years of monthly data or 6 years of quarterly data.
<!-- FORECASTER-FINDER:RULES:END -->

<div class="sk-finder-static" markdown>

**Example script**

The script for one daily series with nothing known in advance. It includes sample data, so it runs as it is, and prints the error of each model.

<!-- FORECASTER-FINDER:EXAMPLE:START - generated by tools/docs/forecaster_finder/build.py, do not edit by hand -->
```python
# pip install skforecast lightgbm chronos-forecasting
# Linux without a GPU? Install PyTorch for CPU first (about 4 GB less):
#     pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from lightgbm import LGBMRegressor
from skforecast.foundation import ForecasterFoundation, FoundationModel
from skforecast.model_selection import (
    TimeSeriesFold,
    backtesting_forecaster,
    backtesting_foundation,
)
from skforecast.preprocessing import CalendarFeatures, RollingFeatures
from skforecast.recursive import ForecasterEquivalentDate, ForecasterRecursive

# Data -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sample data so that the script runs as it is. To use your own data, replace
# this block. For a CSV file with a column of dates and a column of values:
#     data = pd.read_csv("my_data.csv", index_col="date", parse_dates=True)
#     y = data["sales"].asfreq("D")
# "D" is one value per day. If the values turn into NaN after `asfreq`, the
# dates of the file do not match that frequency. If the dates are written as
# day/month/year, add `dayfirst=True` to `read_csv`.
index = pd.date_range("2018-01-01", periods=730, freq="D")
rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
t = np.arange(len(index))
pattern = 0.02 * t + 10 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 7)
y = pd.Series(
    100 + pattern + rng.normal(0, 1, len(index)), index=index, name="sales"
)
dated = isinstance(y.index, pd.DatetimeIndex) and y.index.freq is not None
if not dated or y.isna().all():
    raise ValueError("`y` needs dates with a frequency, and values: check its data.")

# Example settings so that the script runs: they are not tuned.
steps = 14  # days ahead of each forecast
season = 7  # the baseline repeats the same day the week before
# Test: the last 3 forecasts of 14 days each (42 days).
# Every model uses all the data before each forecast.
cv = TimeSeriesFold(
    steps=steps, initial_train_size=len(y) - 3 * steps,
    refit=True, fixed_train_size=False,
)
# Error of each model: the mean absolute error, in the units of your data.
# Lower is better: keep a model only if it beats the baseline.
metric = "mean_absolute_error"

# 1. Baseline: same day the week before
baseline = ForecasterEquivalentDate(offset=season)
error, _ = backtesting_forecaster(baseline, y=y, cv=cv, metric=metric)
print(f"Baseline:  {error[metric].item():.3f}")

# 2. Machine learning: LightGBM with lags, a rolling mean and calendar features
forecaster = ForecasterRecursive(
    estimator=LGBMRegressor(min_child_samples=5, random_state=123, verbose=-1),
    lags=14,
    window_features=RollingFeatures(stats="mean", window_sizes=7),
    calendar_features=CalendarFeatures(features=["day_of_week", "month"]),
)
error, _ = backtesting_forecaster(forecaster, y=y, cv=cv, metric=metric)
print(f"LightGBM:  {error[metric].item():.3f}")

# 3. Foundation model: Chronos-2, no training
# (the first run downloads its weights)
chronos = ForecasterFoundation(estimator=FoundationModel("autogluon/chronos-2-small"))
error, _ = backtesting_foundation(
    chronos, series=y, cv=cv, metric=metric,
    suppress_warnings=True,  # Chronos-2 is not trained: `refit` has no effect on it
)
print(f"Chronos-2: {error[metric].item():.3f}")
```
<!-- FORECASTER-FINDER:EXAMPLE:END -->

</div>
